summary: Psalm 132 begins by asking Yahweh to remember David’s hardships and his vow to find a dwelling place for the Mighty One of Jacob. The psalm then turns to worship at Yahweh’s resting place, asks blessing for priests, saints, and the anointed king, and answers with Yahweh’s sworn promise to David and chosen desire for Zion.
whyItMatters: This chapter joins pilgrimage worship with royal memory: Zion, the ark, priests, poor people, saints, and David’s throne are held together in one prayer. In Book V of Psalms, it looks back to Davidic promise while locating hope in Yahweh’s chosen dwelling and faithfulness.

context.author: No author is named. The heading calls it “A Song of Ascents,” identifying its collection. David is the figure remembered in the poem, not an author named in its heading.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also receiving the Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: Individual psalms may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period. Psalm 132’s precise date cannot be established from its account of David’s vow and Yahweh’s promise alone.
context.setting: Book V of Psalms, among the Songs of Ascents, with Jerusalem/Zion, temple worship, the ark, priests, and Davidic kingship in view.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetry and prayer: compressed lines, repeated petitions and promises, shifts of speaker, and images such as clothing, horn, lamp, throne, and crown.

outline.heading: Remember David’s vow
outline.note: The psalm asks Yahweh to remember David and recalls his vow not to rest until he finds a dwelling for Yahweh.

outline.heading: Seeking the dwelling place
outline.note: The worshiping voice speaks of hearing and finding, then resolves to enter Yahweh’s dwelling place and worship at his footstool.

outline.heading: Prayer for Yahweh’s presence and people
outline.note: The psalm asks Yahweh to arise to his resting place with the ark, and prays for priests, saints, and the anointed one.

outline.heading: Yahweh’s oath to David
outline.note: Yahweh’s promise to David concerns the fruit of David’s body on the throne, with a condition about the children keeping covenant and testimony.

outline.heading: Yahweh chooses Zion
outline.note: The psalm grounds the promise in Yahweh’s choice of Zion as his desired habitation and resting place.

outline.heading: Blessing, joy, and royal hope
outline.note: Yahweh promises provision, bread for the poor, salvation for priests, joy for saints, and honor for David’s anointed while enemies are clothed with shame.

keyVerses.text: Arise, Yahweh, into your resting place, you, and the ark of your strength.
keyVerses.why: This verse gathers the chapter’s central request: Yahweh’s presence, his resting place, and the ark are brought together in prayer.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh has sworn to David in truth. He will not turn from it: “I will set the fruit of your body on your throne.
keyVerses.why: The psalm’s second half turns on Yahweh’s oath to David, so this verse anchors the royal promise behind the prayer.

keyVerses.text: For Yahweh has chosen Zion. He has desired it for his habitation.
keyVerses.why: This verse explains why Zion matters in the psalm: it is presented as Yahweh’s chosen and desired dwelling place.

keyVerses.text: I will abundantly bless her provision. I will satisfy her poor with bread.
keyVerses.why: The promise for Zion is not only royal or priestly; it includes material care for the poor.

themes: Priests clothed with righteousness and salvation
The anointed one, throne, lamp, and crown

questions.question: What is a “Song of Ascents”?
questions.answer: The heading in verse 1 identifies this as “A Song of Ascents.” It belongs to Psalms 120–134, a collection that includes songs about approaching Yahweh’s house. Psalm 132 itself speaks of entering his dwelling place and worshiping there, but it does not specify the ceremony at which the poem was first sung.

questions.question: Why does the psalm ask Yahweh to “remember David”?
questions.answer: The opening petition asks Yahweh to remember David and all his affliction. The next lines define what is being remembered: David swore and vowed not to rest until he found a place and dwelling for Yahweh. The psalm uses David’s devotion as part of its appeal to God.

questions.question: Who is the “Mighty One of Jacob”?
questions.answer: The phrase appears twice in the chapter, both times in connection with Yahweh. Verse 2 says David swore to Yahweh and vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob, and verse 5 speaks of a dwelling for the Mighty One of Jacob. The title links the God addressed here with Jacob, one of Israel’s ancestral names.

questions.question: What is “it” in “we heard of it” and “we found it”?
questions.answer: The pronoun “it” in verse 6 has no explicit noun attached to it in that verse. The surrounding lines concern a dwelling for Yahweh, entering that dwelling, and the ark. That context connects the report of hearing and finding with the search for Yahweh’s resting place, but it does not resolve every detail of the reference or the locations named.

questions.question: What does “footstool” mean here?
questions.answer: Verse 7 says, “We will worship at his footstool.” In the immediate poem, the footstool belongs to Yahweh and is linked with going into his dwelling place. The word pictures worship before Yahweh’s royal presence without requiring the reader to identify every physical detail beyond what the chapter says.

questions.question: Why are priests and saints mentioned together?
questions.answer: Verse 9 prays that priests be clothed with righteousness and saints shout for joy. Verse 16 later answers with Yahweh’s promise to clothe priests with salvation and that saints will shout aloud for joy. The repetition makes priests and saints part of the chapter’s hoped-for restoration and worship.

questions.question: Is the promise to David unconditional or conditional?
questions.answer: The chapter includes both a firm divine oath and a stated condition. Verse 11 says Yahweh has sworn to David in truth and will not turn from it; verse 12 conditions the continuing succession of David’s descendants on their keeping Yahweh’s covenant and testimony. The psalm places divine faithfulness and the descendants’ responsibility together without explaining every implication for later kings.

questions.question: What is Zion in this chapter?
questions.answer: Verse 13 says Yahweh has chosen Zion and desired it for his habitation. Verse 14 calls it Yahweh’s resting place forever and the place where he says he will live. In this psalm, Zion is not just a location name; it is the chosen dwelling place around which blessing, worship, and royal hope gather.

questions.question: What are the “horn,” “lamp,” and “crown” doing at the end?
questions.answer: The final verses use royal images for David’s line and Yahweh’s anointed one. Verse 17 says Yahweh will make David’s horn bud and has ordained a lamp for his anointed; verse 18 contrasts enemies clothed with shame with a crown that will shine on the anointed. Later Jewish and Christian readers often connect Davidic royal language with messianic hope, but this chapter first presents those images within its prayer about David, Zion, and Yahweh’s promise.

glossary.def: The heading attached to this psalm. It identifies the poem as part of a group of ascent songs, though the chapter itself does not explain the exact performance setting.
The sacred object named in verse 8 as “the ark of your strength,” associated here with Yahweh’s resting place.
The place Yahweh is said to have chosen and desired for his habitation in verse 13.
The royal figure in verses 10 and 17, connected in the psalm with David, throne, lamp, crown, and Yahweh’s promise.
